newsitem.title: USA: Employment cost index under scrutiny ahead of FOMC.
newsitem.headline: Employment cost index under scrutiny ahead of FOMC.

text.p: As Federal Reserve policymakers prepare to meet on Tuesday to discuss increasing interest rates, fresh questions are being raised inside and outside the central bank about one of the key indicators that they will be looking at -- the employment cost index (ECI).

The restrained rise of the index -- it showed compensation costs up by just 0.6 percent in the first quarter -- has surprised the Fed and helped convince it not to tighten credit more aggressively in the face of sharply lower unemployment.

While central bank officials generally believe that the index is the best measure of labor costs, some question whether it is fully reflecting wage and other pressures facing employers at this point in the six-year-old expansion.
"The question is whether the ECI is giving the whole cyclical story," said one official, who declined to be named.

Because of the way it is structured, the index does not take account of increased overtime costs. Nor does it take account of workers shifting from lower-paying to higher-paying occupations, as sometimes happens late in an economic cycle.
"You have to wonder whether later in the business cycle if there's a lot of people trading up jobs, people shifting to higher paying occupations," the Fed official said.
Michael Lewis, president of Chicago-based economic consultants Free Market Inc, was far more blunt.
"We believe that recent ECI compensation is downwardly distorted," he said. "Compensation costs are increasing.
Lewis said that recent job gains have been concentrated in high-wage occupations. At the same time, companies have been working existing employees longer, boosting overtime hours.
Neither of those are picked up by the ECI, he added.
Lewis argued that the Labor Department's quarterly productivity report provides a more accurate picture of labor costs than does the ECI.
That report showed that compensation costs increased at an annualized pace of 4.7 percent in the first quarter.

The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets on Tuesday to consider raising interest rates for the second time this year. At its last meeting in March, it raised short-term rates by a quarter percentage point.
